essays.title: The dissociative subtype
essays.sub: On Andrew Laeddis, Shutter Island, and the PTSD that looks like calm instead of chaos
paras: Trauma, I learned, is a wildly overused word. There's a real gap between how casually it gets thrown around and what it clinically means. The example that stuck with me was a car crash: clinical trauma is fundamentally about being out of control. That distinction matters, because trauma and PTSD are not the same thing. What actually pushes a traumatic experience toward a diagnosable condition are specific factors: repetition, interpersonal consequences, exposure, guilt, shame, a pre-existing disorder, and the dependencies that tend to form afterward. Trace all of those far enough and you land on complex trauma, and eventually Complex PTSD, which is standard PTSD layered with emotional dysregulation, interpersonal difficulty, and a deeply negative self-concept.

Dissociation sits right alongside this. Dissociative Identity Disorder is chronic, and depersonalization on its own can actually represent a relatively stable day for someone living with primary psychosis. Both depersonalization and derealization show up more often than people think. Plenty of people use some baseline version of dissociation just to get through a workday. That same low-level dissociation can also come from substances, especially weed and psychedelics, or from a broad range of conditions, notably stress and anxiety. To understand this more precisely, I turned to the DSM-5, which anchored most of what I learned this semester.

Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) requires several criterion to fit the full diagnosis of PTSD, with the necessity of a Criterion A event. A Criterion A event is characterized by direct or indirect exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or events in nature of sexual violence. After a Criterion A event, the DSM-5 organizes the diagnostic features around four different cluster symptoms: Criterion B which covers intrusion symptoms, including involuntary flashbacks and traumatic nightmares; Criterion C addresses continuous avoidance of trauma-related stimulus whether its internal or external; Criterion D covers negative alterations in both cognition and mood, including self-blame, negative emotional state and more; and Criterion E which covers alterations in arousal and reactions, such as hypervigilance and exaggerated startle responses. I was drawn especially to the dissociative subtype specifier that DSM-5 describes on top of these four clusters, which applies when someone with PTSD additionally experiences depersonalization or derealization, the theme I was most interested by. Wikipedia's entry on dissociation in psychology framed it as a spectrum ranging from mild, everyday features all the way to severe changes in identity and memory, which felt eerily familiar to what I'd just learned in class.

In their 2010 peer-reviewed article published in The American Journal of Psychiatry, Lanius et al. set out to display clinical evidence for a dissociative subtype within the larger definition of PTSD. The authors argue that this specific subtype is meaningfully distinct from the general nondissociative form of PTSD. I accessed this article through Northeastern's EBSCO library by simply searching PTSD and dissociation, and I was delighted to find something that researched the exact thing I was describing. Rather than using original data from one singular study, Lanius et al. proceeded to synthesize a multitude of existing neurobiological and clinical evidence in order to build a theoretical model primarily organized around two contrasting patterns of emotional dysregulation within the PTSD diagnosis. The first pattern, which the authors described as emotional undermodulation, characterizes a more traditional presentation of PTSD symptoms, centering around the reexperience and hyperarousal symptoms driven by a failure of prefrontal inhibition of limbic regions. The second pattern, undoubtedly the authors' central contribution, is what they termed emotional overmodulation, and this defines the specific dissociative subtype. In this pattern, the midline prefrontal regions appear to actively inhibit those same limbic areas, producing not a flooding, but instead a suppression. The clinical picture is one centered around depersonalization, derealization, emotional numbing, and a sensation of calmness rather than overt distress. Lanius et al. described these two patterns as a complex dynamic interplay, where patients actively cycle between undermodulated and overmodulated states throughout the course of the disorder. The implications for treatment appear significant: clinicians must assess PTSD patients specifically for this dissociative subtype, because the overmodulated presentation tends to be misread as improvement rather than a distinct symptom profile. The article's central limitation is that its model draws on a body of neuroimaging and literature rather than a single controlled dataset, which the authors themselves acknowledge, framing their conclusion as a proposed model that requires more data rather than a definitive finding.

Shutter Island (2010), directed by Martin Scorsese and adapted from Dennis Lehane's 2003 novel, follows a man presenting himself as U.S. Marshal Edward "Teddy" Daniels, arriving at Ashecliffe Hospital for the Criminally Insane to investigate a missing patient. As the film progresses, it becomes clear that Teddy Daniels is not a real person, and that the actual individual is Andrew Laeddis, a former U.S. Marshal committed to Ashecliffe after the murder of his wife Dolores, who had drowned their three children prior to her murder. Laeddis constructed a full alternate identity with a fabricated professional assignment and a recast of every real person around him. The lead psychiatrist, Dr. John Cawley, explained that this elaborate role-play was permitted as a final therapeutic method before recommending a lobotomy.

Mapping the character profile in Shutter Island against the DSM-5 definition of PTSD and dissociation previously discussed, it appears that every presentation of Laeddis perfectly maps with the DSM criterion of PTSD with dissociative features. His Criterion A event is clear and unambiguous: he had direct exposure to the deaths of his three children at the hands of his wife and moreover proceeded to kill his wife as well, satisfying what DSM-5 identifies as the anchor of the criterion. Laeddis also displays Criterion B symptoms throughout the film, experiencing nightmares through reenactments involving his dead wife, water, and ash, even within the Teddy Daniels persona. Criterion C avoidance, in Laeddis's case, reaches the most remarkable clinical conclusion. Rather than avoiding specific reminders, Laeddis constructed a fully independent identity completely replacing his life with that of Teddy Daniels, eliminating the version of himself who experienced said trauma. Based on the DSM-5 criterion, this is a structural, dissociative avoidance in an extreme form. Interestingly, as Lanius et al. (2010) noted, the fluid relationship between undermodulated and overmodulated symptoms is visible here. You can see it in the relationship between Criterion B and C that Laeddis displays with both a new persona and persistent flashbacks. In regard to Criterion D, the negative cognitions set, it operates beneath the surface but becomes quite significant when more deeply analyzed. In the rare moments where Andrew Laeddis surfaces into reality, you can clearly see the depth of his self-blame over Dolores's untreated illness and the death of his children, and it can even be possible that this Criterion D weight is precisely what creates the necessity for Teddy Daniels's existence, as a form of containment of these deep self-hate symptoms. Criterion E, hyperarousal, seems to manifest as his tactical vigilance, especially as Teddy Daniels. To me, it doesn't seem that Teddy Daniels being an investigator at a mental health hospital is random: he is constantly scanning, forming strategies, and analyzing threats around him, showing a clear nervous system response to a traumatic reality that his mind refuses to acknowledge.

What Lanius et al.'s (2010) model seems to add to this analysis is that of neurological coherence. Andrew does not present the flooded, overtly distressed profile that popularly defines PTSD, specifically in movies. What Lanius et al. describes as the overmodulation signature is precisely what the film depicts. If it would be possible to scan Laeddis's brain, it would theoretically show midline prefrontal inhibition of limbic activity in such an extreme way that experiential reality has been fully reorganized. It is worth noting that I would not identify Laeddis to have DID, as there seems to be no co-existing alters, no clear amnesia barriers between distinct states. There is instead a complete identity replacement, placing him more directly within PTSD with dissociative tendencies in an extreme manner. Dr. Cawley temporarily breaks through this system, and Andrew briefly reclaimed his actual identity, even acknowledging his trauma, further supporting a PTSD reading over DID. The final scene reverses this, as Andrew questions whether it was better to live as a monster or to die as a good man, signalling a deliberate return to Teddy Daniels with awareness that a lobotomy will follow. The analysis of Shutter Island made me more prone to agreeing with the conclusions of Lanius et al., as cases such as this do demand recognition as a distinct clinical representation, because to many it can look like progress from traditional PTSD, when in reality it's just a deeper and different presentation of its symptoms.
essays.source: Lanius, R. A., et al. (2010). Emotion modulation in PTSD: Clinical and neurobiological evidence for a dissociative subtype. The American Journal of Psychiatry, 167(6).

essays.title: Horses, not zebras
essays.sub: On cyclothymic disorder, and why the common explanation is usually the right one
paras: I became fascinated with cyclothymic disorder the day I heard it described as "heavily underdiagnosed." In class, a chart went up on the board mapping the full spectrum of mood: euthymia as the normal baseline, hypomania rising subtly above it, and mania above that, loud and unmistakable, usually ending in a hospital or a jail cell. Below the baseline came dysthymia, summed up in one blunt word: "meh." Further down, Major Depressive Disorder, graded from mild to severe. Once the whole spectrum was mapped, cyclothymic disorder appeared as the pattern that moves quietly between dysthymia and hypomania, cycling for at least two years, sometimes shifting with the seasons.

It felt more personal than Bipolar I and II ever had. I'm not claiming I have cyclothymic disorder, but the shift between periods of hyperactivity and periods of just feeling "meh" seemed more relatable than anything else on that chart, if only because ordinary euthymia already comes with its own ups and downs. What actually clicked for me was a line borrowed from an old piece of medical wisdom: "when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras." That's when I understood why cyclothymia gets missed so often. Practitioners are trained to look for Bipolar I and II, and the quieter, more common pattern hiding in plain sight goes unnoticed.

To understand the diagnosis more precisely, I accessed DSM-5-TR through the library page. According to DSM-5-TR, cyclothymic disorder is categorized as a chronic, fluctuating disorder with hypomanic and depressive features while not meeting full episode criteria, requiring two years for diagnosis. DSM-5-TR specifies that if after this period the patient experiences a manic or major depressive episode, they receive another diagnosis, whether Bipolar or Major Depressive Disorder. DSM-5-TR also notes that cyclothymic disorder is prevalent in 0.4-2.5% of the population with typical onset in adolescence or early adulthood, and interestingly around 15-50% of cases lead to a full bipolar diagnosis. To go deeper, I consulted Wikipedia's page on cyclothymia, which introduced the theme of comorbidity: adolescent cyclothymic disorder is typically associated with ADHD, anxiety, eating disorders, or impulse control issues. The ADHD connection especially caught my attention, which led me to an article examining both conditions directly.

In their 2021 study published in Medicina, Giulio Emilio Brancati and colleagues investigated the relationship between cyclothymic disorder and ADHD, examining whether emotional dysregulation is a potential overlapping feature. The researchers aimed to examine comorbidity rates between the two diagnoses and explore emotional dysregulation patterns among diagnostic groups. Brancati et al. recruited 165 patients from a psychiatry unit in Pisa, Italy, dividing them into three groups: 80 ADHD patients, 60 with cyclothymic disorder, and 25 with both diagnoses. The authors measured temperament using the TEMPS-M scale and emotional dysregulation using the RIPoSt-40 questionnaire, assessing four facets: affective instability, positive emotionality, negative emotionality, and emotional impulsivity. The study revealed that approximately one-fourth of ADHD patients met cyclothymic disorder criteria, and one-third of cyclothymic patients were diagnosed with ADHD, showing major overlap between the two. Both groups had similar levels of emotional dysregulation overall. However, cyclothymic patients without ADHD showed more negative emotionality, depression, and anxiety compared to those with ADHD, while ADHD patients showed more hypomanic symptoms with higher rates of substance abuse. Patients with both diagnoses scored highest in affective instability. The authors acknowledged that recruiting from a clinical setting may have skewed toward more complicated, higher-comorbidity cases, and that their cyclothymic criteria were more inclusive than DSM-5's, which may have captured patients who don't meet the full diagnostic threshold. Still, Brancati et al. concluded that both conditions are heavily related to emotional dysregulation, with cyclothymic disorder trending toward depression and anxiety and ADHD trending toward hypomanic features, and that more positively leaning cyclothymic individuals might go undiagnosed unless ADHD symptoms are also present.

What struck me most was that finding: cyclothymia trending more negative than ADHD despite comparable dysregulation overall. My best guess connects directly to the authors' point about "positive leaning" cyclothymic patients slipping through undiagnosed. The most likely explanation is that people whose mood swings lean positive simply don't get diagnosed, or don't show up in a clinic at all. They just live with it. If most cyclothymic patients who do seek treatment present with depressive or anxious features to begin with, that raises a real question: does cyclothymia actually trend negative, or is it just underdiagnosed whenever it trends positive?

This makes even more sense once you sit with how underdiagnosed cyclothymia actually is. I suspect clinicians aren't only primed to search for Bipolar or Major Depressive Disorder over cyclothymia. They're also more readily primed to search for ADHD in general. And if a patient's mood swings lean positive without any accompanying ADHD symptoms, they're less likely to seek help in the first place, which means they simply stay undiagnosed. This is the "horses, not zebras" principle in practice: clinicians tend to search for the diagnoses they've been trained to expect, not necessarily the ones that are actually most prevalent. One thing this study taught me is that emotional dysregulation could serve as a strong baseline factor for diagnosing both conditions, since Brancati et al. showed comparable rates across both groups. That overlap suggests clinicians should be screening ADHD patients for cyclothymic disorder and vice versa, a practice that could catch conditions that would otherwise go unnoticed. It might even be worth using the more commonly diagnosed ADHD population as an entry point for catching missed cyclothymia cases before they progress into full bipolar disorder.
essays.source: Brancati, G. E., et al. (2021). Comparison of Emotional Dysregulation Features in Cyclothymia and Adult ADHD. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania), 57(5).

essays.title: La violencia y su legitimidad
essays.sub: Sobre la autoridad, los derechos individuales y las cláusulas 39 y 40 de la Carta Magna
paras: La Carta Magna es un documento firmado por el rey de Inglaterra y un grupo de barones rebeldes en 1215 donde se limitaba el poder de la corona y del monarca. Esta carta y este documento legal fueron escritos a través de una presión violenta, que causó que el rey fuera obligado a firmar. Fue la primera vez en la historia humana donde el gobierno o la autoridad fue limitada y la primera vez donde se otorgaban derechos inalienables a los ciudadanos, sentando así bases para los gobiernos limitados y los derechos individuales en todos los sistemas políticos que precedieron a 1215. Las cláusulas 39 y 40 mencionan específicamente que los ciudadanos no pueden ser castigados si no es por una corte, dándoles completo derecho a un juicio y a defenderse, y quitándole a la corona el derecho absoluto de castigar sin límites. En otras palabras, estas cláusulas representan una afirmación explícita de derechos individuales ante una autoridad que antes era total.

Elijo este objeto específicamente porque encarna la tensión que quiero explorar de la manera más literal posible: es un documento que otorga derechos individuales permanentes, pero cuyo origen es inseparable de la violencia que lo produjo. No se puede leer la cláusula 39 sin leer también la rebelión armada de los barones que la hizo posible. Esa es la razón por la que el objeto no es solamente un ejemplo ilustrativo, sino el punto de partida necesario de la pregunta filosófica: si el resultado (derechos individuales permanentes, un límite real al poder de la corona) es defendible, ¿eso legitima retroactivamente el medio violento que lo produjo? Y si no lo hace, ¿qué estatus filosófico le queda a un documento fundacional cuyo origen fue ilegítimo? Con estas dos filosofías y la cláusula 39 y 40 de la Carta Magna, donde se establece la libertad ante una autoridad, se podrá responder la pregunta: ¿Es legítima la violencia como medio para alcanzar o modificar la autoridad y establecer derechos individuales?

La primera perspectiva filosófica es la de Hannah Arendt, quien en su libro Sobre la Violencia inicia una indagación profunda sobre la relación inherente entre la violencia y la autoridad. Arendt distingue tres términos: la autoridad, el poder y la violencia. Para Hannah Arendt, la autoridad implica un reconocimiento legítimo de gobernar, es decir, algo es una autoridad cuando es reconocida como algo legítimo con el derecho de gobernar, donde preferiblemente se basa en el consentimiento. El poder es la capacidad de las personas para trabajar juntas con consentimiento y legitimidad, es decir, el poder es lo que se puede crear a través de la cooperación legítima. La última definición que propone Hannah Arendt es la de la violencia, que según ella es una herramienta que puede forzar la obediencia del pueblo pero que nunca puede establecer legitimidad. Arendt determina que "Políticamente hablando, es insuficiente decir que poder y violencia no son la misma cosa. El poder y la violencia son opuestos" (Arendt 77). Esto significa que cuando existe el poder no existe la violencia, y cuando el poder no se tiene, se infiltra la violencia. Finalmente, la definición más importante de Hannah Arendt es la de la legitimidad; para Arendt, la legitimidad de un gobierno o autoridad consiste en el establecimiento de leyes y documentos y el consentimiento y cooperación del pueblo durante su creación.

Utilizando ejemplos históricos, Arendt demuestra que a lo largo de la historia muchas autoridades han conseguido lo que quieren a través de la violencia, pero también argumenta el otro lado: que muchos ciudadanos han conseguido lo que quieren a través de la violencia y movimientos de revolución. Arendt hace el argumento de que la violencia no es una manera buena para establecer autoridad. Menciona que la violencia en muchos casos obliga a muchos a someterse a la autoridad, pero que es una solución a corto plazo que no garantiza una autoridad a largo plazo; más bien, por lo general se relaciona la violencia con una brecha hacia nuevas formas de opresión y dominación física. Arendt luego hace el debate entre el poder y la violencia, encontrando su relación pero también sus claras diferencias: el poder se establece a través de la legitimidad y del consentimiento de un pueblo, mientras que la violencia obliga a seguir a la autoridad poderosa a través de la fuerza, sin consentimiento y de manera ilegítima. Arendt critica la violencia como forma de conseguir lo que se quiere políticamente, y aboga por el diálogo, la discusión y los movimientos pacíficos como formas mucho más poderosas de conseguir la autoridad y promover el cambio social.

Con base en esta reconstrucción se puede contestar la pregunta filosófica principal del ensayo. Para Hannah Arendt, la violencia simplemente no es una manera legítima para alcanzar o modificar la autoridad, ni para modificar la libertad de los ciudadanos. Arendt argumenta más bien por otras formas de llegar a la autoridad que sean legítimas. Ella admite que la violencia es eficaz, pero no cree que sea una manera legítima de conseguir o modificar la autoridad o la libertad. Sin embargo, en relación con las cláusulas 39 y 40 de la Carta Magna, las ideas de Arendt encuentran un problema real. Los precedentes de la Carta Magna fueron conseguidos a través de traición y violencia, algo que Arendt calificaría de ilegítimo; sin embargo, la violencia aquí no fue usada para alcanzar la autoridad desde cero, sino para modificarla y para modificar la libertad de los ciudadanos ya existentes. Arendt iría en contra de esta modificación por considerarla ilegítima en su origen, aunque estaría de acuerdo con la idea primordial de fijar esos derechos de manera escrita y oficial una vez conseguidos.

La teoría de Hannah Arendt es muy completa y argumenta que la violencia no es una manera legítima de conseguir la autoridad, ya que es solamente una herramienta para obligar o forzar a la gente a seguir algo, lo cual significa que no existe consentimiento. Arendt dice que "la práctica de la violencia, como toda acción, cambia el mundo, pero el cambio más probable originará un mundo más violento" (Arendt 110). Sin embargo, la idea de Arendt tiene una dificultad real para explicar situaciones históricas donde un cambio positivo y duradero sí surgió a través de la violencia, como en la Revolución Francesa, la cual llevó a Francia, y a movimientos similares alrededor del mundo, a producir resultados que hoy consideramos positivos, como la Declaración de los Derechos del Hombre y del Ciudadano. La teoría de Arendt es completa y relevante para la pregunta filosófica del ensayo, pero deja sin resolver estas excepciones históricas.

Ahora se analizará a Étienne de la Boétie, específicamente en su Discurso de la Servidumbre Voluntaria. Étienne de la Boétie comienza explicando lo que es la libertad: la libertad individual es un derecho inherente a todos los individuos, es decir, es de todos y todos nacen con ese derecho. La sumisión a un tirano, a un poder corrupto que interfiere con esta libertad individual, ocurre a través de una sumisión voluntaria, que en sí misma es una contradicción al derecho de la libertad. La verdadera libertad implica tomar decisiones completamente propias sin estar bajo la influencia o prohibición de un gobierno tirano.

Étienne de la Boétie también dice que el poder solo existe porque los ciudadanos permiten que suceda. Argumenta que quitar a una autoridad tirana para conseguir la libertad deseada es fácil, pero muchos se someten y no pelean por su libertad, permitiendo que sistemas de autoridad malos existan y continúen. Como dice en su libro, "resulta, pues, que la libertad es natural y que, en mi opinión, no sólo nacemos en posesión de nuestra libertad, sino también con la inclinación a defenderla" (de la Boétie 57). Aquí se argumenta de manera explícita que el humano nace con la libertad, pero también agrega que el humano siempre va a tener el derecho, el poder y el deseo de defenderla. Con eso dicho, también argumenta que "tantos hombres, tantos pueblos, tantas ciudades, tantas naciones soportan en alguna ocasión a un tirano solo, cuyo poder surge del que ellos le quieran dar; que solo puede hacerles daño mientras quieran soportarlo" (de la Boétie 45). Aquí se ve cómo de la Boétie piensa que la libertad es algo fácil de conseguir y que cuando se quita esta libertad es fácil volver a conseguirla, pero a pesar de eso, muchos se rehúsan a hacerlo por otras razones.

Usando a Étienne de la Boétie para responder la pregunta filosófica principal, se puede encontrar que para él la violencia es sin duda una manera legítima de conseguir o modificar la autoridad y cambiar la libertad, completamente en desacuerdo con las teorías de Hannah Arendt. De la Boétie argumenta que cualquier tipo de movimiento o estrategia para quitar a un tirano y proteger la libertad es necesario y un derecho fundamental en sí mismo. En relación con las cláusulas 39 y 40, esto es extremadamente claro: durante la rebelión que las produjo, se garantizaron derechos de libertad a través de una rebelión armada, lo cual se alinea directamente con las ideas de de la Boétie, ya que la sociedad quiso conseguir sus derechos a ser tratados bajo corte y a defenderse del castigo de un gobierno tirano. Esto demuestra que, en realidad, la sociedad le da el poder a la autoridad, y que el poder que esta tiene existe porque la sociedad lo permite.

La perspectiva filosófica de de la Boétie es muy clara: el pueblo puede y debe hacer todo para proteger la libertad. Concuerdo con la idea de que la protección de la libertad es un derecho fundamental del pueblo; sin embargo, de la Boétie no menciona los sacrificios de libertad que el pueblo mismo tiene que hacer para que la sociedad funcione. Cuando un nuevo gobierno o una nueva autoridad se establece, sea a través de la violencia u otros medios, el pueblo tiene que someterse y seguir las leyes del nuevo gobierno, sacrificando a su vez algún tipo de libertad. De la Boétie ignora esto por completo, pero es fundamental para entender si un movimiento armado puede realmente cambiar la libertad sin generar nuevas formas de limitación: la respuesta sería que sí puede, pero con límites reales.

Antes de proponer mi propia síntesis, vale la pena considerar la objeción más fuerte contra cualquier intento de legitimar la violencia a través del consentimiento posterior, viniendo de una tradición distinta a la de Arendt o de la Boétie: la del monopolio de la violencia de Max Weber. Desde esta perspectiva, la legitimidad de un uso de la fuerza no depende realmente del consentimiento del pueblo en el momento de la violencia, sino de si esa fuerza logra establecer, después del hecho, un monopolio reconocido y estable sobre el uso legítimo de la violencia dentro de un territorio. Bajo esta visión, mi propia conclusión, que la violencia puede ser legítima cuando es precursora de procesos democráticos con consentimiento, podría ser cuestionada: ¿qué pasa si el consentimiento posterior no es más que la aceptación resignada de quien ya no tiene manera de resistir al nuevo monopolio de fuerza? La Revolución Francesa es un ejemplo perfecto de esta tensión. Si bien produjo la Declaración de los Derechos del Hombre y del Ciudadano, también produjo el Terror, un período donde la violencia continuó mucho después de que la autoridad tiránica original hubiera sido derrocada, y donde miles de personas fueron ejecutadas sin el tipo de juicio legal que las cláusulas 39 y 40 de la Carta Magna buscan garantizar. Esto complica cualquier lectura simple de la Revolución Francesa como un caso exitoso de violencia legitimada por el consentimiento; el mismo evento que uso como evidencia a favor de mi posición contiene dentro de sí un contraejemplo directo a esa posición.

Considero que esta objeción es seria pero no decisiva. Weber tiene razón en que el monopolio de la fuerza, una vez establecido, puede sostenerse sin necesitar consentimiento activo y continuo. Pero la pregunta filosófica de este ensayo no es si la violencia puede sostener una autoridad, sino si puede legitimarla, y esas son preguntas distintas. El Terror no invalida la legitimidad de la Declaración de 1789; más bien demuestra exactamente el límite que yo mismo quiero trazar: la violencia deja de ser legítima en el momento en que se separa del proceso democrático que decía estar sirviendo. La Revolución Francesa no es, entonces, un solo caso, sino dos: una fase donde la violencia fue precursora de un proceso legal y de consentimiento real (y por lo tanto legítima, según mi criterio), y una fase posterior donde la violencia se volvió un fin en sí misma, sin consentimiento ni proceso legal (y por lo tanto ilegítima, incluso según mi propio criterio). Esta distinción es, creo, más útil que la de Arendt o de la Boétie por separado, porque ninguna de las dos teorías por sí sola logra explicar por qué la misma revolución puede contener un momento legítimo y un momento ilegítimo.

Principalmente, estoy de acuerdo con las definiciones de Hannah Arendt sobre la autoridad, la legitimidad y el poder. Sin embargo, creo que la violencia sí puede ser una herramienta para conseguir autoridad de manera legítima cuando da lugar a procesos legales democráticos, como leyes y votaciones, con el consentimiento del pueblo, y solamente mientras dure esa conexión con el proceso democrático. La Revolución Francesa, leída con el cuidado que la objeción weberiana exige, es un ejemplo de ambas posibilidades a la vez: cómo la violencia puede establecer una autoridad de manera legítima, y cómo esa misma legitimidad puede perderse cuando la violencia se independiza del consentimiento que la justificaba.

Con respecto a los derechos individuales, la respuesta es la misma. Como dice de la Boétie, el pueblo tiene el derecho y la obligación de pelear por su libertad. Con eso dicho, también es importante entender que todo cambio en la libertad y los derechos individuales tendrá consecuencias futuras, y que toda autoridad tiene que regular los derechos individuales en algún grado. La violencia puede ser una manera legítima de conseguir y cambiar derechos individuales siempre y cuando cuente con el consentimiento de la mayoría, sea precursora de procesos democráticos, y se detenga en el momento en que ese proceso democrático queda establecido. La violencia debe ser la última herramienta para conseguir la autoridad; el diálogo y los procesos establecidos deberían ser preferibles, como piensa Arendt, porque esos siempre son legítimos. La violencia no debe ser la primera opción, pero el pueblo tampoco debe tener miedo de usarla para proteger su libertad, siempre que sepa reconocer el momento exacto en el que debe detenerse.
essays.source: Arendt, Hannah. Sobre la violencia. Penguin Books, 2023. De la Boétie, Étienne. Discurso de la servidumbre voluntaria. Virus Editorial, 2016.

essays.title: What resilience is not
essays.sub: On self-esteem, self-efficacy, and the difference between bouncing back and being unaffected
paras: Self-esteem and self-efficacy get taught as if they're two sides of the same coin, but they aren't quite that simple. Self-esteem comes down to confidence in your own worth, abilities, and values: a mix of belief and emotional state. Mental health disorders directly erode it, and that erosion is a large part of why stigma around mental illness persists the way it does. I liked one metaphor for it: self-esteem as a gas tank. A full tank supports daily functioning and makes treatment possible. What surprised me was the follow-up point: there's no real benefit to a fantastic tank over a merely good one. My instinct is that better is always better, especially for something like self-esteem, but once you sit with the definition, the marginal gain between "good" and "great" self-confidence doesn't do much extra clinical work. Negative self-esteem, on the other hand, isn't just a symptom. It's a barrier to recovery in its own right.

Self-efficacy works differently. There's no such thing as too much of it. The more the better. It's the ability to set goals and actually follow through on them, which lines up with Maslow's hierarchy of needs, particularly self-actualization. It develops observationally and vicariously, shaped heavily by parenting style, and mental illness directly undermines a person's capacity to build it in the first place. Both concepts eventually point toward the same destination: meaningfulness. That connects to Seligman's PERMA model, five components that drive well-being: positive emotions, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment. I kept coming back to meaning specifically, which Seligman describes as belonging to or serving something larger than yourself. That's the piece that ties everything together. Meaning is what keeps someone working after they've already gotten the material things and experiences they wanted. It's the throughline underneath a well-established sense of self-efficacy.

In Usán Supervía et al.'s 2025 study published in SAGE Open, a peer reviewed journal, the researchers investigated the relationship between the themes of self-efficacy, resilience, and self-esteem. The researchers focused on adolescent secondary school students, and used a specific lens on whether resilience can mediate the relationship between self-efficacy and self-esteem. The study involved 1,968 participants ranging from ages 12-18 from nine schools in Zaragoza, Spain, and they were selected through simple random sampling. Usán Supervía et al. measured the academic self-efficacy of the participants using the Academic Self-Efficacy Scale, resilience through the Brief Resilience Scale, and self-esteem using the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, which are all validated for Spanish adolescents. The researchers began by examining gender differences, finding that while males scored higher in self-efficacy and self-esteem than females, none of these differences in the results reached any statistical significance. Usán Supervía et al. then conducted a correlational analysis, highlighting that resilience strongly correlated with self-efficacy and more modestly with self-esteem, while self-efficacy and self-esteem showed a more modest positive correlation. Most importantly, the authors implemented a mediation analysis and found that self-efficacy did not directly predict self-esteem in a statistically significant way, but that resilience fully mediated this relationship. Therefore, self-efficacy appeared to build self-esteem indirectly by first strengthening resilience. Usán Supervía et al. acknowledged some key limitations: the cross-sectional design prevented any causal conclusions, and the sample, while large, lacked diversity and only represented one Spanish city, so whether these results are replicable elsewhere is unknown. The authors concluded that fostering resilience in academic settings is essential, because it serves as the psychological component connecting a student's belief in their abilities and their overall sense of self-worth.

What resilience actually means mattered to me personally. Growing up in Mexico City's heavily patriarchal "macho" culture, I'd been exposed to a lot of what gets called resilience that was really just repression dressed up as toughness, and it was nothing but harmful. So when I read that the Brief Resilience Scale measures someone's capacity to bounce back from hardship rather than how unaffected they are by it, I needed to sit with that distinction before I could take the study's conclusions seriously. Once I confirmed the two weren't the same thing, I could actually engage with what the authors were arguing. Their broader claim, that reinforcing resilience is a meaningful way to improve both self-esteem and self-efficacy, holds up logically. But I think they leave too much out. For secondary school students, things like physical self-image, social status, wealth, and parenting style all shape self-esteem and self-efficacy in ways a study like this can't fully capture. And the finding that self-efficacy doesn't directly predict self-esteem clarified something else for me too: why those two concepts get taught as separate, related but distinct, rather than as the same thing wearing two names.
essays.source: Usán Supervía, P., et al. (2025). Exploring the Mediating Role of Resilience in the Relationship between Self-Efficacy and Self-Esteem in Adolescent Secondary School Students. SAGE Open, 15(3).

essays.title: The weight of "meh"
essays.sub: On Carl Fredricksen, the elderly widower from Pixar's Up, and the difference between depression and just not wanting to
paras: There's a particular chart that stayed with me all semester, what I came to think of as a Chart of Episodes. Picture a vertical axis of mood states. At the top, mania: no sleep, psychotic features, usually lasting around a week, usually ending in a hospital or a jail cell. Just below it, hypomania: more subtle, less sleep, often genuinely productive and even enjoyable while it lasts, though there's always a crash waiting on the other side. At the baseline sits euthymia, ordinary functioning. Below that, dysthymia, summed up in a single word: "meh." Not a soft depression, but a persistent low state that colors everything for a long stretch of time, the clinical anchor for Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD). Further down, a Major Depressive Episode: two weeks, graded by severity. Mild means you can't fully function day to day, moderate means multiple areas of your life are impaired, severe means you can barely get out of bed, and severe with psychotic features anchors Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) itself. Anxiety and its related symptoms live at the bottom of this same chart too, which is part of why so many anxiety disorders get treated with the same medications as depression. Bipolar I and II sit elsewhere on the chart, alongside cyclothymia, which I've written about elsewhere. But going into this piece, I kept returning to that one word: "meh." The explanation itself felt like the thing it was describing.

To understand these diagnoses more precisely, I went to the DSM-5. Persistent Depressive Disorder is a depressed mood occurring most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years, alongside two or more of: poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, poor concentration, and an overall sense of hopelessness. A gap longer than two months without these symptoms within that two-year window disqualifies the diagnosis. Major Depressive Disorder differs by being episodic rather than chronic: five or more symptoms over a two-week period, representing a real departure from prior functioning, with depressed mood or anhedonia as one of the required symptoms. The rest of Criterion A includes significant weight change, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue, excessive guilt, and recurrent thoughts of death. Criteria B and C require that the episode cause real distress or impairment, unrelated to substances or medical conditions. There's a spectrum within MDD itself too, more symptoms, more intensity, more severity, up to and including psychotic features. Alongside these two, I came across Prolonged Grief Disorder (PGD), a grief response disproportionate in both intensity and duration, persisting twelve months or more after the loss. What distinguishes it from ordinary grief is its persistence and its interference with daily functioning: a lasting longing for the deceased, alongside at least three of the following: disruption to identity, disbelief about the death, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, prolonged difficulty reintegrating into life, emotional numbness, a sense that life is meaningless without the deceased, and an intense loneliness. PGD is distinct from MDD and from normal grief, and the two can coexist.

To go deeper, I found a narrative review published in Frontiers in Psychiatry, written by Wang and Feng in 2022, titled "A Narrative Review of Empirical Literature of Behavioral Activation Treatment for Depression." The authors trace Behavioral Activation to two foundational models. The first is the response-based reinforcement model, grounded in the work of Lewinsohn and Ferster, which states that depression is caused and sustained by the loss or reduction of positive reinforcement. Secondly, the action-based model adds that low reward expectation by itself results in sustained depressive behavior by diminishing motivation to act. Together, both models give Behavioral Activation its central clinical target. The authors highlight the TRAP pattern (trigger, response, avoidance), where avoidant behavior reduces positive reinforcement, deepens the depression, and produces further avoidant behavior, creating a self-sustaining loop. Following TRAP is TRAC: trigger, response, alternative cope, which breaks the cycle by reintroducing a structured set of rewarding activities into a person's life, regardless of whether motivation exists first. The sequencing matters, because Behavioral Activation does not wait for mood to improve before introducing activity. It proposes that activity itself drives the mood change. Wang and Feng identified evidence across a range of depressed populations: a ten-week Behavioral Activation intervention for patients diagnosed with MDD or dysthymic-related disorders produced medium to large effects compared to normal treatment, with Cohen's d values ranging from 0.70 to 1.02. For depressed inpatients, a BATD format produced a Cohen's d of 0.75 compared to supportive psychotherapy. Behavioral activation was also effective in alleviating grief, PTSD, and depressive symptoms in a middle-aged bereaved population, producing a Cohen's d of -1.19, a notably large effect, with significant improvements also found in elderly individuals in similar circumstances. The evidence for behavioral activation's effectiveness is increasing, though the authors note a clear limitation: most of it is tied to specific protocols proposed by Martell et al. or Lejuez et al., which raises the question of whether it's behavioral activation itself, or the protocols, doing the work.

I analyzed Carl Fredricksen, the elderly widower at the center of Pete Docter's Pixar film Up (2009). The film opens with an emotionally charged montage collapsing Carl and his late wife Ellie's entire life into a few minutes: falling in love, building their home, dreaming about traveling to Paradise Falls, grieving a miscarriage, saving money and spending it and saving again, growing old together, and then the abrupt quiet as we watch Ellie pass away. After the montage, we follow Carl as a solitary, grumpy old man facing forced relocation to a retirement facility after several legal altercations with construction workers. A young, enthusiastic Wilderness Explorer named Russell nags Carl relentlessly to earn his last merit badge. That nagging eventually leads them to tie ten thousand balloons to Carl's house, finally reaching Paradise Falls, with Russell earning his badge along the way.

Applying the DSM criteria to Carl directly, several diagnostic considerations present themselves. He shows no apparent motivation, complete social withdrawal, hostility toward neighbors, and a stubborn refusal to engage with anything outside his own home. Pinning down a single diagnosis is genuinely difficult. The film implies a long stretch of time has passed since Ellie's death, which points toward Prolonged Grief Disorder, though it's impossible to know whether that stretch clears the twelve-month threshold. Carl's central characteristic maps directly onto "meh": he doesn't feel like doing anything, and simply lives that way. Major Depressive Disorder is also a fully reasonable read.

I lean toward Persistent Depressive Disorder as the best-fitting diagnosis, alongside features of Prolonged Grief Disorder. The case for PDD rests on the chronic nature of his behavior: a constant low mood that the film suggests has lasted a long time. His flatness of affect, withdrawal, and hostility don't read as a discrete onset. They read as simply how he's lived since his wife died. There's a real gap in the evidence, since DSM requires two or more years of depressive symptoms on most days, and the film withholds the exact timeline, which makes a precise diagnosis impossible. Carl's life before her death matters here too. He was heavily engaged with living meaningfully, with nothing signaling a pre-existing depression. Even the miscarriage, an earlier hardship, seems to have been something he grieved and recovered from alongside Ellie. It's the inability to do that same thing without her that reinforces the PGD I believe is present. That said, MDD can't be ruled out either. The severity of his impairment, the near-institutionalization, and the way he keeps the house as a shrine to her all fit DSM criteria for MDD just as well. A clearer timeline would help enormously. Absent that, it's the chronic, persistent "meh" quality of his behavior that leans me toward PDD with features of PGD.

The connection to behavioral activation is the most clinically interesting part of this. As the movie progresses, Carl does get better. Reading Wang and Feng, it's hard not to see Russell's relentless nagging and pushing as an unplanned form of behavioral activation. Whether it's just talking, keeping Carl company on the porch, or floating away to Paradise Falls, Russell keeps supplying Carl with exactly what he's been depriving himself of: the TRAP pattern in reverse. As Russell slowly gets Carl to do more and more, culminating in the deeply positive reinforcement of actually reaching Paradise Falls, Carl improves. That's the TRAC pattern in action: a relationship disguised as behavioral activation becomes genuinely therapeutic. Russell giving Carl a concrete goal gives him something to look forward to, sparking a positive reinforcement loop. Carl's stubbornness toward Russell isn't incidental. It's the TRAP pattern playing out in real time, and Russell's persistence is what inadvertently breaks it.

The resolution of Up isn't just a satisfying ending. It's a clinically coherent example of behavioral activation in practice, one that even addresses the main limitation Wang and Feng identified about relying on structured protocols. One of the most enjoyable parts of the film is that it's a child doing this: Russell's nagging hands Carl his life back, giving him renewed energy and letting him take control of his emotions again. Carl improves, but he isn't cured. He just shows real direction and a lighter severity of symptoms. He never actually talks about Ellie's death, and the film doesn't give his grief a therapeutically satisfying resolution. What stayed with me is that persistent feeling of "meh," and then, slowly, watching Carl improve through a form of behavioral activation he never asked for, brought entirely by a persistent eight-year-old boy scout who couldn't take no for an answer.
essays.source: Wang, X., & Feng, Z. (2022). A narrative review of empirical literature of behavioral activation treatment for depression. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 13.
